newsitem.title: UK: British Conservative MPs discuss election defeat.
newsitem.headline: British Conservative MPs discuss election defeat.

text.p: Efforts by senior British ministers to rally their Conservative Party for a drive to win an imminent election were torpedoed on Friday by MPs indulging in public speculation about what would happen if they lost.

While one of the party's legislators urged Prime Minister John Major to step down as party leader immediately after an election defeat, another said he should stay on because some of his potential successors could lose their seats and would have to wait for by-elections to re-enter parliament.
The comments came as party members gathered in Bath, western England for a rally designed to give them heart for the electoral battle.

While finance minister Kenneth Clarke attacked Labour's economic spokesman Gordon Brown for indecisiveness, former minister Edwina Currie was speculating on BBC radio about what would happen in the aftermath of a defeat.
Currie said manoeuvring ahead of a post-election leadership contest was already under way. "There is already a great deal of formation of columns and lines and factions and groups," she said.

If Labour came to power, the best option would be for the contest to follow immediately, Currie said. "Please, John, please don't make us hang around. Please don't make us wait. Can we please get on with it."
But another MP, John Biffen, said the Conservatives' defeat could be so great that senior cabinet members who might want to fight such a contest would no longer be MPs.
"There might then be a case to wait until by-elections can be held to remedy that situation," he said.
The speculation about defeat came within seven weeks of the expected May 1 date of a general election, and after an opinion poll showed Labour 25 points ahead of the Conservatives.

It earned an apparent rebuke from party chairman Brian Mawhinney, who told the Bath meeting: "Every sinew, every waking moment for all in our party must now be devoted exclusively to winning the election."
"To every Conservative, one message -- if you don't have something to say that will help us win, don't say anything at all."
The controversy overshadowed Clarke's speech in which he said Britain would take a holiday from economic history if it elects a Labour government.
Clarke said under Labour, Britain would turn its back on the liberalising economic approach which he claimed was starting to make it a role model for the world.

He added: "If you vote Labour, you call a halt to tax-cutting, you vote for higher spending, you give more powers to the (trade) unions...voting Labour means an end to the economic reform agenda which has transformed Britain from basket-case to role model."
